title: Design Review Slides — Mixed-workload scheduler prototype (short/long prompt-aware scheduling)
content:
Slide 1 — Title
Mixed-workload scheduler prototype (Serving Runtime Performance: Kernel + Scheduling)
Design review (prototype behind flag)
Owners: Sofia Ivanova / Lena Fischer

Slide 2 — Why we’re here (motivation)
- Customer-reported issue: p95/p99 latency spikes for interactive chat traffic during long-context windows (summarization, RAG, batch jobs)
- Observed pattern: queue + prefill contention dominates tails; decode-only throughput looks fine on averages
- We can’t rely on “more GPUs” as the primary fix for Dedicated tiers; we need stable tail behavior under mixed prompt lengths
- Goal of prototype: prioritize latency-sensitive work without starving throughput-heavy work; make behavior predictable + observable

Slide 3 — Problem statement
When long context requests (prefill-heavy) are co-scheduled with short interactive requests:
- FIFO / opportunistic batching can put short requests behind long prefill batches
- Short requests’ end-to-end latency becomes “coupled” to the longest prompt in the batch
- Bursty arrivals trigger oscillations: queue depth growth, batch size growth, even worse tail

Slide 4 — Success criteria (draft)
Primary
- Reduce mixed-workload p95 E2E latency for short/interactive class by 30–50% in representative distributions
- Keep throughput regression within acceptable bound (initial gate: <= 5% tokens/sec drop on steady-state mixed suites)
- Fairness: long requests must not starve (bounded wait time; measurable guardrail)
Secondary
- Stable behavior under burst (no unbounded queue growth due to policy)
- Operator visibility: per-class queue depth/wait time; ability to debug “why was this request delayed?”

Slide 5 — Non-goals (prototype)
- Not rewriting kernels; minimal kernel changes only to prevent measurement artifacts
- Not changing customer-facing API behavior
- Not introducing per-customer bespoke routing logic (we will allow tier hints later, but policy should stand on its own)

Slide 6 — Workload taxonomy (what we mean by “mixed”)
Two classes for prototype (can evolve later)
- SHORT (latency-sensitive): typical chat turns, small RAG prompts, tool calls
  - High sensitivity to queueing delay; usually small prefill
- LONG (throughput-heavy): summarization, long-context ingest, eval/batch jobs
  - Prefill dominates service time; tolerates higher latency but needs throughput + fairness
Note: We classify by expected prefill cost, not just token count (token count is our safe starting proxy)

Slide 7 — Where tail latency comes from (mixed workload)
E2E latency decomposition (common case):
- Queue wait time (scheduler + admission)  ← biggest lever
- Prefill time (long contexts)              ← workload-dependent; also batching-dependent
- Decode time (streaming)                  ← relatively stable for short prompts
- Runtime overhead (locks, dispatch, tracing)

Slide 8 — Example timeline (why FIFO fails)
Scenario: long prompts arrive, form a large prefill batch; short requests arrive slightly after

Time →
Queue:  [L1][L2][L3][L4]...[Lk] [S1][S2][S3]
Dispatch (FIFO-ish + batch fill):
- Prefill(L1..Lk) runs (hundreds of ms to seconds depending on context)
- Short requests S1–S3 wait behind full prefill batch
Result:
- Short p95 balloons even though GPU is “busy doing useful work”

Slide 9 — Design intent
We want a policy that:
- Gives short requests a fast path most of the time
- Prevents long starvation (explicit bound)
- Avoids pathological oscillations under burst (stable queueing)
- Remains compatible with continuous batching + existing kernel selection

Slide 10 — Options considered (high level)
1) FIFO
- + Simple
- - Tail coupling; worst-case short latency equals long prefill window

2) SRPT approximation (shortest remaining processing time)
- + Theoretically good for mean/queueing
- - Hard to predict remaining time accurately; noisy; risk of starvation without careful aging

3) Two queues (SHORT priority with fairness window)
- + Simple; predictable; easy to reason about starvation
- + Good match to “short interactive vs long batch” reality
- - Needs good classification + tuning to avoid long throughput collapse

4) Token-based fair queueing / WFQ
- + Cleaner fairness
- - Implementation complexity; interactions with batching; requires robust per-request cost accounting

Slide 11 — Proposed prototype policy (two-queue + fairness window)
Core idea
- Maintain two ready queues: Q_short and Q_long
- Dispatch rule (simplified):
  - Prefer Q_short
  - But service Q_long at least once per fairness window (or if Q_short empty)

Parameters (initial)
- fairness_window_ms: e.g., 50–150ms target; “don’t let long wait forever”
- max_short_burst: optional; cap consecutive short dispatches
- long_min_share: optional; minimum service rate for long under continuous short arrivals

Why this form
- Easy to implement behind flag
- Easy to instrument
- Easy to explain to SRE + customers as “short gets priority, long is bounded”

Slide 12 — Starvation bounds (how we make this safe)
Guardrails we want in v0
- Max long wait bound target (soft): p99 wait_time_long should not exceed X seconds under defined load
- Hard policy: after fairness window elapses, next eligible dispatch must consider Q_long even if Q_short is non-empty
- Overload mode: admission control by class (so long doesn’t inflate short queueing and vice versa)

Slide 13 — Classification heuristics (v0)
Initial conservative classifier (safe default)
- Classify as LONG if prompt_tokens >= threshold
- Otherwise SHORT
Threshold candidates
- Start: 1,024 tokens (tunable per model / hardware)
- Alternative: 768 for smaller GPUs where prefill scales worse

Planned improvements (after we have stable instrumentation)
- Predict prefill cost using:
  - prompt_tokens * model-specific coefficient
  - rolling EWMA of observed prefill time (per route/model) with safeguards
- Optional hints (later): request priority tier / customer tier / route tags

Failure modes to watch
- Misclassification: “long but labeled short” can wreck short queue
- Distribution drift: threshold tuned on one workload, fails on another

Slide 14 — Dispatch + batching interactions (key concern)
Key risk: if batching logic builds a prefill batch including long prompts, short can still get stuck behind the batch
Mitigation direction
- Maintain class-aware batch formation (don’t mix long prefill into a short batch)
- Ensure scheduler decision happens before batch assembly
- Regression test: “short request should not be blocked behind long prefill batch”

Slide 15 — Backpressure / admission control (prototype plan)
Why
- Under overload, queue depth can grow; tail latency explodes; policy becomes irrelevant
Plan
- Separate admission control thresholds by class
  - Q_short: lower depth threshold, protect latency
  - Q_long: allow deeper queue but cap to avoid memory pressure
- Expose signals: reject_rate_by_class, queue_depth_by_class

Slide 16 — Observability we need (must-have)
Metrics (per class)
- queue_depth (gauge)
- enqueue_rate / dequeue_rate
- wait_time_ms (histogram)
- service_time_ms (histogram)
- prefill_time_ms vs decode_time_ms split
- starvation events (counter): “wait exceeded threshold”
Tracing
- Span annotations: class, enqueue_ts, dequeue_ts, dispatch_reason (short-priority vs fairness)
Debug logging (sampled)
- “scheduler decision record” for on-call investigation

Slide 17 — Benchmark plan overview
Suites
- Synthetic distributions
  - Bimodal: 80% short (<=256 tokens), 20% long (2k–8k tokens)
  - Heavier long tail: 60/40 split
  - Burst tests: short bursts during long wave
- Trace replays
  - Representative customer-like traces from perf lab (anonymized)

Metrics
- p50/p95/p99 E2E for short + long
- Throughput (tokens/sec) overall
- GPU utilization + batching stats
- Queueing breakdown

Slide 18 — Preliminary results (synthetic, early; not yet gated)
Hardware: A100 80GB (single node), Model: Redwood-verified 7B baseline profile
Workload: 80% short (128–256), 20% long (4096–8192), steady arrival

Table (baseline FIFO-ish vs two-queue prototype)
- Short p50: 210ms → 220ms (+5%)
- Short p95: 1.85s → 0.92s (-50%)
- Short p99: 3.10s → 1.60s (-48%)
- Long p95: 7.8s → 8.6s (+10%)
- Throughput: 100% → 97% (-3%)

Interpretation
- Large tail win for short class
- Small throughput hit within our initial bound
- Long latency increases slightly but remains within expected tolerance; must ensure long doesn’t starve under continuous short

Slide 19 — “Graph” (ASCII) to visualize tail shift
Short E2E latency CDF (lower is better)

Latency (ms)  | 500 | 1000 | 1500 | 2000 | 2500 | 3000
Baseline FIFO |  *  |  **  |  *** | **** | *****| ******
Two-queue     | *** | *****| ****** (flatter tail)

(Real plots will be published via benchmark runner output once PR lands in benchmark-lab)

Slide 20 — What improved (hypothesis)
- Short requests no longer wait behind long prefill windows
- Queue wait time histogram for short shifts left substantially
- Less “batch hostage” behavior (but only if we avoid class-mixing in batch formation)

Slide 21 — What got worse / open questions
- Long p95 increased in some scenarios (expected trade-off)
- Under extreme short-heavy load, long progress relies entirely on fairness window tuning
- Threshold sensitivity: a 768 vs 1024 cutoff changes long queue composition materially
- Interaction with streaming: long streaming decode can still consume slots; we need to be clear what we prioritize (prefill vs decode)

Slide 22 — Stability under burst (what we’re testing)
Test scenario
- Background: long prompts steady
- Spike: 30s burst of short requests at 2–3x normal rate
What we want to see
- Short p95 stays bounded; queue_depth_short drains promptly
- Long queue depth increases but remains controlled; after burst, long drains with predictable slope
- No oscillatory batching (batch size runaway)

Slide 23 — Rollout plan (flagged)
Runtime version target: 1.19 (default OFF)
Stages
1) Perf-canary A/B (flag off vs on)
2) Limited production slice (Dedicated internal + opt-in customers)
3) Expand to more routes once pass/fail gates are satisfied
Rollback triggers (draft)
- Short p95 regression > 10% in any guard scenario
- Starvation alerts: long wait_time p99 exceeds bound for > N minutes
- Queue depth growth without recovery (sustained slope)

Slide 24 — Decision points for this review (what we need agreement on)
1) Is two-queue + fairness window the right v0 policy to prototype?
2) Classification: is prompt_tokens threshold acceptable as a conservative starting point?
3) Fairness definition: do we commit to a hard policy bound (window) vs “best effort”?
4) Benchmark gates: confirm acceptable throughput regression bound for prototype stage
5) Instrumentation scope: any missing metrics required for SRE sign-off?

Slide 25 — Risks & mitigations
Risk: misclassification causes short queue pollution
- Mitigation: conservative thresholds; fallback to FIFO if anomaly detected; add metric for “short queue long-prefill outliers”

Risk: priority inversion via batching implementation
- Mitigation: class-aware batch assembly; regression test; tracing for dispatch_reason

Risk: lock contention / overhead from per-class queues
- Mitigation: measure scheduler CPU time; keep critical section small; sample logs

Risk: unfairness to long leading to customer pain on batch jobs
- Mitigation: explicit fairness window + guardrail metrics; communicate expected trade-off

Slide 26 — Implementation plan (what’s landing)
Phase 1 (week 3–5)
- Feature flag plumbing + config surface
- Classifier module (token threshold)
- Two-queue dispatch logic + fairness window
- Basic metrics + tracing hooks

Phase 2 (week 5–7)
- Backpressure per class
- Benchmark harness updates + CI gate draft
- Tuning threshold + fairness window

Phase 3 (week 7–9)
- Canary A/B + dashboard panels
- Fixes from canary; decision ADR

Slide 27 — Current status (as of last edit)
- Spec: draft complete; needs feedback on fairness + gates
- Code: PRs in progress (flag + classification + dispatch)
- Bench: Rina setting up mixed workload runner output format
- SRE: request is “metrics first”; want clear rollback triggers and starvation alert

Slide 28 — Asks / reviewers
- Runtime scheduling: validate dispatch logic + fairness semantics (Lena, Marcus)
- Kernel consult: confirm no pathological kernel selection triggered (Hiro, Grace, Yuki)
- Perf program: confirm benchmark methodology + gating (Jonas, Rina)
- SRE: agree on dashboards + rollback triggers (Sean, Rafael, Aisha)

Slide 29 — Appendix: terminology (quick)
- Prefill: processing prompt/context tokens (often dominant for long context)
- Decode: token generation phase (streamed); tends to be steadier per token
- Mixed workload: concurrent short interactive + long prefill-heavy requests on same scheduler/GPU pool

Slide 30 — Appendix: concrete parameter strawman
Initial defaults (flag ON only)
- long_prompt_threshold_tokens: 1024
- fairness_window_ms: 100
- long_min_share: 10% dispatch opportunities (soft)
- admission_control
  - max_queue_short: 2x target_concurrency
  - max_queue_long: 6x target_concurrency
Notes
- These are placeholders; will be tuned using mixed suite + trace replay

Speaker notes (general)
- Emphasize that this is a prototype for tail stabilization; default-off and carefully gated.
- Be explicit about trade-off: slightly worse long latency can be acceptable if short tail is protected, but long starvation is not acceptable.
- Ask SRE to define “starvation” in operationally meaningful thresholds (minutes? seconds?) per tier.
- Confirm whether we should treat streaming decode as latency-sensitive for SHORT (likely yes) and how to avoid long decode hogging.
